generatedProse.concept-context: In practice, self-regulated learning shows in how you approach a piece of work in any subject. Rather than reading until a deadline forces a result, a self-regulating student sets a clear goal, chooses a strategy, checks part-way whether the work is building towards that goal, and judges the finished piece against the standard. Across disciplines, it is this deliberate, monitored approach that steady improvement rests on.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two students with four weeks to complete the same demanding assignment.

Student A starts straight away and keeps working as material accumulates, with no goal beyond covering the topic and no check on whether the argument is building, until the work comes back with a disappointing result. Student A was busy throughout, but never stood back to monitor or adjust. This is working without regulating.

Student B begins by setting a goal: a clear position, supported by the strongest evidence, finished early. Student B chooses what to focus on, checks at the halfway point whether the argument holds, and drops a line that is not working. Afterwards Student B notes what to do differently next time. This is self-regulated learning: forethought, performance and evaluation, run on purpose.

Both students worked hard. Only Student B drove the process, and it is Student B who will improve from one task to the next.
generatedProse.summary: Self-regulated learning means driving your own work through forethought, performance and evaluation: setting a goal and strategy, monitoring whether the work is building, and judging the result against the standard. You can now explain the process and recognise it in how a student approaches a task. The next lesson turns to one tool of self-regulation: judging your own work against the marking criteria.

check.body: What makes a student self-regulating rather than simply hard-working?

items.text: Setting a goal, monitoring whether the work is building, and adjusting the approach along the way.
Spending more hours on the task than anyone else.
Starting the reading earlier than other students.
Asking for more guidance before beginning.

feedback.correct: That's right. Setting a goal, monitoring the work and adjusting the approach is self-regulation in action.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what a self-regulating student does with the process, beyond working hard.
feedback.incorrectFinal: A student is self-regulating when they set a goal, monitor whether the work is building, and adjust the approach. Extra hours, an earlier start or more guidance are not the point.

_prompts.concept-context: What does this look like in practice within the given context? Write a short follow-on from the generic definition above, in the learner's own subject or discipline. Keep it to two or three sentences, mid-register, following straight on from the generic definition.
_prompts.worked-example: Give a subject-specific worked example of this lesson's concept: a weaker or less-developed version first, then a stronger version reached by better practice, using the context cast (character tokens) consistently. Keep the weaker-then-stronger shape and the two-part contrast; carry the cast only through the {{learner-a}} (weaker) and {{learner-b}} (stronger) tokens, never a literal name (the pack supplies the whole body, but not the names). Each example paragraph must begin with its token, weaker first - merge-context.js's wrapProse() only emits the we-weaker/we-stronger cue classes for a paragraph that leads with the token. The merge renders it as a block quote, so write it as continuous prose, not as a quoted comment plus commentary.
_prompts.summary: Recap what the learner can now do, in terms of their own subject or context. One short paragraph. Do not restate the learning outcomes verbatim.
_prompts.check: Write the subject's own version of this lesson's check question(s), testing the same outcome in the learner's own discipline. Keep the same number of items and the same correctness pattern as the generic version; reword the stem and items for the subject. Keep the component-level feedback (correct / notFinal / final) teaching, never a bare verdict.
